newsitem.title: UK: EMI to prepare for EMU reserves despite debate.
newsitem.headline: EMI to prepare for EMU reserves despite debate.

text.p: The European Monetary Institute (EMI) will prepare plans for reserve requirements under a single European currency, despite the heated debate over whether they are needed, an EMI official said on Thursday.
Speaking at a conference on the implications of EMU for international debt markets, Paul Mercier, head of financial markets at the EMI said time restraints demanded quick action.

"There is still strong debate over reserve requirements, with some countries saying they are not needed," said Mercier. "We must prepare the system to be ready at the start, even though we don't know whether it will be used."
The German central bank has argued strongly that the future European central bank, which will replace the EMI, should use reserve requirements as part of its monetary policy toolbox.

The Bundesbank is the only European central bank with significant minimum reserve requirements and many banks outside of Germany fear they will be penalised if these are introduced at the launch of EMU in January, 1999.
German banks must contribute between 1.5 and 2.0 percent of short-term borrowings obtained from foreign banks or domestic non-banks to non-interest bearing accounts at the Bundesbank.
Mercier said central reserves, if they were used, would not be held in addition to national systems. A decision on this issue would have to be made by late 1997 or early 1998 at the latest, he said.
"We must have uniform rules throughout the union," he said.
Analysts at the conference said they envisaged a system where small insitutions would be exempt from the reserve requirements.
Mercier said the ECB would establish a lombard facility, with a rate slightly above the market rate, and a deposit facility with a rate under market rates.
"It is through this corridor that we will try to steer interest rates," he said.
The ECB would start to execute all its operations in euros from January 1 1999, he said.
"The EMI is currently writing the blueprints of monetary policy," he said.
Mercier said that although policy decisions would be taken centrally, the ECB would rely on national central banks for their expertise in their own markets.
"Only in exceptional circumstances will the ECB intervene directly," he said. "There will be a single monetary policy with separate branches carrying it out."
Other decisions -- from the type of collateral acceptable as reserve requirments to the mechanism for the issuance and distribution of bank notes -- had yet to be taken, Mercier said.
But it was expected that a framework report would be published by late 1996 or early 1997.
"That will contain enough information for us to make a good start," he said.
